title: Chess: A Sport for the Mind
summary: How chess is played, where it came from, and why it is treated as a real sport today, including in Saudi Arabia.
poll: Chess should count as a real sport.

versions.title: A Game for the Mind
versions.text:
Two kids sit at a board. They do not run. They do not kick a ball. But they work hard. They play chess!

The board has 64 squares. Each side has 16 pieces. There is a king and a queen. There are pawns and more. Each kind of piece moves in its own way.

The goal is to trap the king. If the king can not get away, the game ends. That is checkmate.

To win, you need a plan. You must think a few moves ahead. What will your foe do next? You must guess.

Chess is very old. It came from India long, long ago. Then it went to Persia. Then it went all through the Arab lands. Then the world got it.

Chess is now a sport. Some games use a clock. In 2017, top players came to play in Riyadh.

You can play, too. All you need is a board and a friend.

To win, you need a good plan. You must think a few moves ahead. You must guess what the other player will do.

Chess is very old. It began in India long ago. Then it spread to Persia and to the Arab lands. From there, it went all over the world.

Today, chess is a real sport. Many games use a clock. In 2017, the best fast players in the world came to Riyadh to play.

You can play chess, too. All you need is a board and a friend.

Two students sit across from each other at a small table. They are not running, jumping, or kicking a ball, yet their minds are working extremely hard. They are playing chess, an ancient game that many people describe as a sport for the mind.

A chess board contains 64 squares, and each player begins with 16 pieces: a king, a queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. Every type of piece moves differently, and a player captures an opponent's piece by moving onto its square.

The objective is to trap the opposing king. When the king is attacked and has no possible escape, the game ends in checkmate, a word derived from the Persian phrase shah mat, which is often translated as "the king is helpless."

Winning requires a clear strategy, intense concentration, and careful planning. Experienced players calculate several moves ahead, and they try to anticipate what their opponent will do so that they can prepare an effective response.

Chess originated in India approximately 1,500 years ago. It subsequently spread to Persia and across the Arab world, where accomplished players such as as-Suli, a celebrated master in Baghdad, wrote about the game and composed challenging puzzles. Later, chess traveled to Europe and eventually around the globe.

Today, chess is a competitive sport with clubs, professional coaches, and international tournaments, and the International Olympic Committee has officially recognized it as a sport. Players frequently use a special clock, which forces them to think quickly. In 2017, Riyadh hosted a world championship for rapid and blitz chess, two accelerated forms of the game.

Many educators believe chess helps students focus and plan carefully. Best of all, anyone can begin, because all you need is a board and a willing friend.

Two students sit across from each other at a small table. They are not running, jumping, or kicking a ball, yet their minds are working extraordinarily hard. They are playing chess, an ancient game that many people describe as a sport for the mind.

A chess board contains 64 squares, and each player begins with 16 pieces: a king, a queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. Every category of piece moves differently, and a player captures an opponent's piece by moving onto its square.

The objective is to trap the opposing king. When the king is attacked and has no possible escape, the game concludes in checkmate, a term derived from the Persian phrase shah mat, which is frequently translated as "the king is helpless."

Victory requires intense concentration and meticulous planning. Experienced players calculate numerous moves ahead, and they attempt to anticipate their opponent's intentions so that they can prepare an effective response.

Chess originated in India approximately 1,500 years ago. It subsequently spread to Persia and across the Arab world, where accomplished players such as as-Suli, a celebrated master in Baghdad, analyzed the game and composed challenging puzzles. Eventually, chess traveled to Europe and ultimately around the globe.

Today, chess is a competitive sport with clubs, professional coaches, and international tournaments, and the International Olympic Committee has officially recognized it as a sport. Competitors frequently use a special clock, which compels them to make decisions quickly. In 2017, Riyadh hosted a world championship for rapid and blitz chess, two accelerated variations of the game, attracting many of the planet's strongest players.

Modern players also train with powerful computer programs, which can evaluate millions of positions every second. Nevertheless, human competitors still depend on memory, intuition, and patience, because no player can calculate every possible continuation during an actual game.

Numerous educators believe chess helps students concentrate and plan carefully. Best of all, anyone can begin, because all you need is a board and a willing friend.
